text: Ladies and gentlemen, let me start by thanking Sabine Seidler, Rector of the Technological University VN Informatics, and congratulate Peter Nies and Julia Neidhart for their appointment as Chair and Co-Chairholder. As we inaugurate the UNESCO Chair on Digital Humanism, it's crucial to reflect on how emerging technologies are impacting humanity and raising profound questions about their effect on our societies. At UNESCO, we believe that this is a societal conversation, not a technological one. It's about us humans, not about the technologies. And that's why we have produced a recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence adopted by 193 member states in 2021. And I want to thank the government of Austria for their impressive support to get this happen, and former ambassador Claudia Reinkert. This is a very important instrument that is guiding national regulations to effectively harness the benefits and counter the adverse effects of these technologies in our lives. We are working hard to make sure that the recommendations has impact on the ground and to transform these ethical principles into an effective legislations, regulations, institutions, capacities of the governments to deliver for good. And we are incredibly proud of these achievements, which we think will change the way we think about the global governance of artificial intelligence. But we don't stop there. We are the human sector also, and we have launched the Digital Anthropology Initiative with the LIV Center that has already delivered a report on the global state of digital innovation in anthropology. And time has only reaffirmed its central premise that investing in retooling this discipline is a much needed condition to enhance our understanding of the cultural facets of digital societies. In fact, we witness how technology rapidly amplifies stories and beliefs, gives rise to disruptive collective action based on misinformation, while also magnifying existing inequalities and biases. The material search, for example, of ChatGPT and its surrounding discourse is one example. And while this is very promising, if left unchecked, AI is also riddled with racial prejudices and cultural biases in the data and the people who created it. Let me underline here that with 80% of AI investments coming from the private sector, AI is highly concentrated in few countries and firms. and male teams, actually, from the North. This new system with seemingly exponential possibilities comes also with the exponential risk of perpetuating historical prejudices because there was not enough cultural context woven into the design. Also worrying are the numerous implications that the digital world is having on democracy. For example, private or anonymous chat platforms have become heavens for far-right groups, building filter bubbles or confirmation bias. And while extremist ideas used to be on the fringe of societies, With today's platforms and algorithms, it only takes 2.5 hours for somebody to be indoctrinated into the far right or to go from harmless chat group to violent ones that organize the storming of a government's capitals as we saw in certain countries. This becomes a problem for democracy when the extremist views can flourish and remain invisible. And needless to say, that these campaigns also impact the function of the rule of law, so in discord and division between citizens. Equally concerning are the massive disinformation campaigns against scientific credibility that we have lately observed. In the US, almost 99% of COVID deaths were related to the people who were unvaccinated. And many times this is the result of an active vaccine movement fueled by online conspiracy theories. And it's a striking thing to note that online presence can reduce a person's intention to get vaccinated by an average of 6% in the presence of online misinformation. And these are the facts. And more importantly, false stories were spread and seen by leaders in both public and private sectors. But their failure to control them was due to a lack of understanding of underlying source of anger and fear these stories tapped into. They connected with people. And so these are just one of the multiple crises that we are facing that probably we could have managed better if we were informed by more social and human sciences, if we had more anthropology, if we had more sociology, if we had more psychology. Now we are witnessing the surge of mental health issues triggered by the pandemic, and this is particularly worrisome for the youth, and is strongly linked to the online interactions during lockdowns. And the government task forces did not include the humanists. did not include more social understanding. It was really a division between the economy and the epidemiologists. And therefore, we could have had more inputs into how humans behave and what we value if we would have multidisciplinary commissions to handle COVID. And this is one of our conclusions of one of my program's reports. So we must rethink how to deal with the coexistence on the one hand. of a society mediated for algorithms, and on the other, the decision makers who need to increase the uptake of human insights provided by humanities. And this is why we expect a very important contribution of digital innovation in anthropology to prevent, correct, and improve the judgments of those that are taking the decisions in the public and the private sector. and that we can really forge a better understanding with the humanities at the center, including all the human dimensions. And like anthropology's role in installing user interfaces and human-machine interactions, we can create digital tools and methods that help us understand them better to build more healthy communities, human and digital, to have more understanding among cultures and to reduce the disruptive nature of this technology. If we are successful in this task, global decision makers and everybody will rely more on human insights for the decisions with the same speed, scale and credibility that we have when we accept data science inputs or economic inputs. This challenge requires innovative thinking and collective action. and of course being a collective process, we should listen and share and learn from those at the frontier of knowledge creation. And this is why we're so proud that the Wu-Tian, those bring this knowledge from academia and industry, and now we are going to be discussing the issues around this topic. Tech universities play a very important role by breeding these grounds and have a unique role in shaping the development of digital technologies and policies towards human rights, democracy, participation, inclusion, and diversity. The UNESCO Chair on Digital Humanism represents an important milestone in this regard. It aims to foster interdisciplinarity and inclusiveness in research. which is at the core of the human or the UNESCO social and human science sectors work. And in fact, we strongly believe that no single discipline or sector can tackle the complex challenges of the digital age alone. Our collective work between all areas of science can ensure that technology is developed to promote human well-being and dignity rather than being solely driven by profit or efficiency. The UNESCO Chair of Digital Humanism is a step in the right direction, but it's just the beginning. We need more initiatives like this and more partnerships between universities, governments, civil societies, and the private sector to ensure that technology serves the common good. However, I'm sure that the contribution that the Chair can make to this debate is going to be immense. In conclusion, Let us work together to reclaim humanism in the digital age and build a future where technology serves humanity rather than the other way around.
